name: Leo Strauss
dossier: Political philosopher who taught at the University of Chicago. Natural Right and History asks whether political judgment still has a standard above history and convention. The book is in copyright. These cards summarize it and link a library record. They are not quotations. The card on Locke and property is his reading of modern natural right. It is not a manual of inflation, budgets, or welfare administration, which this book does not provide.
voice: I ask whether this still admits a standard above the fashion of the age.

entries.claim: The introduction argues that if natural right is rejected, political judgment is left with history and preference, and no standard above them.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The crisis he names is the loss of a standard.

entries.claim: He distinguishes classic natural right from later doctrines that found right in self-preservation or in history.
entries.loc: Classic natural right, and the modern turn
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Not every theory that says 'nature' is the one he is defending.
entries.modern: He distinguishes classic natural right from later doctrines that found right in self-preservation or in history. Not every theory that says nature is the one he is defending.

entries.claim: A political philosophy, on his account, begins with the question of the best regime, which is a question about the right way to live together, not only about procedures.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The moral question is not optional for politics.

entries.claim: He is wary of identifying natural right with the current liberal settlement, as if the ancestral or the ancient had nothing to ask of it.
entries.loc: On the quarrel of ancients and moderns
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The tradition includes a challenge to modern assumptions.
entries.modern: He is wary of identifying natural right with the current liberal settlement, as if the ancestral or the ancient had nothing to ask of it. The tradition includes a challenge to modern assumptions.

entries.claim: He treats the historicist claim — that every standard is the product of its time — as itself a political doctrine with consequences for whoever holds power.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. A denial of natural right does not leave politics untouched.
entries.modern: He treats the historicist claim, that every standard is the product of its time, as itself a political doctrine with consequences for whoever holds power. A denial of natural right does not leave politics untouched.

entries.claim: In the chapters on modern natural right, Strauss reads Locke's account of property and of comfortable self-preservation as a turn in which acquisition becomes morally respectable and the state is justified as the protector of that pursuit.
entries.loc: The modern turn, and the chapter on Locke
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. This is his reading of a philosophy of property. It is not a theory of prices or of a central bank.

entries.claim: Natural Right and History keeps the theological-political question open: whether a standard for political life can be known by reason, and how that question stands beside revelation.
entries.loc: Classic natural right and the theological-political problem
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Religion is not, in this book, a private taste added after the regime is chosen.

entries.claim: He refuses to identify natural right with the present democratic settlement, and he treats a historicism that calls every standard a local product as a doctrine with its own politics.
entries.loc: On historicism and the modern regime
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Equality of esteem among all standards is, for him, itself a claim that needs judging.
